title: Human variants that break Watson-Crick pairs of 483,913 predicted conserved RNA structures are not rarer than pair-keeping variants; an apparent signal at G-U pairs is the same on both DNA strands
abstract:
In human genetic variation, the base pairs of predicted conserved RNA structures in non-coding DNA show no sign of natural selection on pairing. This matters because genome-wide structure predictions were used to claim that a large part of the human genome is under selection for RNA structure.

We tested 483,913 conserved RNA structures (CRSs, Seemann et al. 2017) and 34,159 EvoFold structures against single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) in 76,215 genomes (gnomAD v4.1). At each predicted pair we compared SNVs that break the pair with SNVs that keep it (for example C to U opposite G, which makes a G-U pair). Logistic models matched SNVs for 192 RNA-strand mutation classes and mammalian conservation; decoy pairs moved along the same structures gave the baseline. The odds ratio (real / decoy) is below 1 if pair-breaking SNVs are missing.

At Watson-Crick pairs (G-C, A-U; 86% of pairs), non-coding CRSs gave 1.000 (95% interval 0.996-1.005; 1.001 at non-CpG sites): 1.002 where a gene is transcribed from the predicted strand, 0.999 where only the other strand is transcribed, 0.999 without a gene. At CpG sites the ratio was 1.039, the opposite direction to selection. At G-U pairs they gave 0.956 (0.942-0.969) on both strands alike, through an excess of transitions that make the pair Watson-Crick; this excess grows with the share of other species that carry that Watson-Crick pair (odds ratio 1.29 at 75-100% vs under 25%), while pair-breaking SNVs do not change, which marks recurrent mutability. Selection on RNA pairing acts only on the transcribed strand, and a pair-keeping change on one strand is pair-breaking on the other, so this is not RNA-level selection; it makes a naive all-pairs test report 2% selection on structure. For CRSs inside one gene, the predicted strand is the gene strand in only 52.8%. RNA folds of random intron DNA gave 1.015 (0.996-1.035). Known structured RNAs gave 0.84-0.93 with wide intervals (tRNA genes, 0.81, reflect hypermutation), so a share of selected pairs cannot be bounded.

Thus any extra loss of pair-breaking SNVs at CRS Watson-Crick pairs is below about 0.5%. Population tests of predicted RNA structure should treat G-U pairs and CpG sites apart and use a strand control. Limits: gnomAD detects only selection of about 1e-3 or stronger per site, so weak selection on some pairs is not excluded; two of four controls were chosen after first results; the set of Smith et al. (2013) that covers 13.6% of the genome was not tested directly.

display.caption: Pairing tests by pair type. Odds ratio of being observed in gnomAD v4.1 for pair-breaking vs pair-keeping SNVs, real / decoy structure, from logistic models matched for 192 RNA-strand mutation classes and mammalian conservation; below 1 means pair-breaking SNVs are missing. (a) Watson-Crick pairs: CRSs in all transcription contexts are at 1.0. (b) G-U pairs: CRSs are below 1 on both strands alike. Orange: known structured RNAs (pre-specified or post hoc controls); blue: CRS by context; green: EvoFold; grey: RNA folds of random intron DNA (grey band: its interval). Bars: 95% delete-one-chromosome jackknife intervals, t(21).

The G-U artifact. (a) At predicted G-U pairs, transitions that make the pair Watson-Crick are in excess relative to decoys at non-CpG sites, equally on the transcribed strand and on the other strand, and not in random folds. (b) At Watson-Crick pairs, pair-keeping and pair-breaking SNVs are equally rare relative to unpaired bases in CRSs; in EvoFold structures on small ncRNA genes, pair-breaking SNVs are rarer. (c) At human G-U pairs, pair-keeping transitions become more common the more other species carry a Watson-Crick pair in the same columns; pair-breaking SNVs at the same bases do not change (jackknife 95% intervals).

Strand tests. (a) Ratios of Watson-Crick pairing effects between CRSs on the transcribed strand and CRSs on the other strand or outside genes are all near 1; dashed orange lines mark the point estimates of two controls. (b) The predicted CRS strand matches the strand of the overlapping gene in only 51-54% (EvoFold 54-60%).
